Three child proposals were accepted into the pending queue; the fourth was rejected (maxChildren limit reached), so I will cover atomic broadcast and impossibility results directly, and — since no child outputs have been returned to me — I will synthesize the full brief myself to guarantee complete, rigorous coverage of all eight areas.

# Technical Brief: Distributed Consensus and Coordination

---

## 1. Raft

Raft (Ongaro & Ousterhout, 2014) decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety, maintaining the **State Machine Safety** property: if any server applies a log entry at a given index, no other server ever applies a different entry at that index.

**Mechanism 1 — Leader election with randomized election timeouts.** Time is divided into monotonically increasing **terms**, each with at most one leader. A follower that receives no heartbeat (empty **AppendEntries RPC**) within its election timeout transitions to **candidate**, increments its `currentTerm`, votes for itself, and issues **RequestVote RPCs**. A candidate wins upon receiving votes from a majority; each server grants at most one vote per term (persisted as `votedFor`), which guarantees the **Election Safety** property (≤1 leader per term) via quorum intersection. **Randomized election timeouts** (e.g., 150–300 ms) break the split-vote livelock probabilistically, which is Raft's practical answer to FLP (see §8).

**Mechanism 2 — Log replication and the Log Matching Property.** The leader appends client commands to its log and replicates via AppendEntries, which carries `prevLogIndex`/`prevLogTerm` as a **consistency check**. The induction this enforces yields the **Log Matching Property**: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical up through that index. Divergent follower logs are repaired by the leader decrementing `nextIndex` and overwriting conflicting suffixes; followers are strictly passive. An entry is **committed** when the leader has replicated it on a majority in its current term, advancing `commitIndex`, which propagates to followers and drives `lastApplied` on the state machine.

**Mechanism 3 — Safety restrictions: the election restriction and current-term commitment.** A voter rejects RequestVote unless the candidate's log is at least as **up-to-date** (higher last term, or equal last term and ≥ length). Combined with quorum intersection this yields the **Leader Completeness Property**: a leader for term *T* contains all entries committed in terms < *T*. Crucially, a leader may only count replicas to commit entries **from its own term** (Figure 8 of the Raft paper shows the counterexample otherwise); entries from prior terms are committed *indirectly* once a current-term entry on top of them commits. Practical systems (etcd) have the new leader append a **no-op entry** at term start to commit the prefix promptly and to enable **ReadIndex**-based linearizable reads.

Supporting mechanisms: **log compaction via snapshotting** (`InstallSnapshot RPC`), **Pre-Vote** (a candidate probes electability before incrementing its term, preventing disruptive term inflation by partitioned nodes), and **CheckQuorum/leader stickiness**.

---

## 2. Paxos

**Mechanism 1 — Single-Decree (Synod) Paxos.** Lamport's protocol decides a single value among **proposers**, **acceptors**, and **learners** in two phases over **proposal numbers** (ballots), totally ordered and unique per proposer. **Phase 1a (Prepare)**: a proposer sends `prepare(n)`. **Phase 1b (Promise)**: an acceptor that has not promised a number > n replies with a promise never to accept proposals numbered < n, attaching the highest-numbered proposal it has already **accepted**, if any. **Phase 2a (Accept)**: upon promises from a majority, the proposer proposes the **value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported**, or its own value if none — this is the heart of Paxos safety. **Phase 2b (Accepted)**: acceptors accept unless they have promised a higher number. A value is **chosen** when a majority accepts it; safety follows from **quorum intersection**: any two majorities share an acceptor, so a chosen value is visible to every later Phase 1. Liveness is not guaranteed (dueling proposers can livelock), consistent with FLP; a **distinguished proposer** elected via Ω restores liveness.

**Mechanism 2 — Multi-Paxos.** For a replicated log, running full two-phase Synod per slot is wasteful. Multi-Paxos elects a **stable leader** that executes Phase 1 **once for infinitely many instances**, then runs only Phase 2 per log slot (one round trip, like Raft's steady state). Standard engineering additions: a **window/α of concurrently open instances**, filling gaps with **no-ops**, and distinguished learner routing. Chubby, Spanner, and ZooKeeper's conceptual lineage all sit atop Multi-Paxos-style replication.

**Mechanism 3 — Variants generalizing quorums and ordering.**
- **Fast Paxos** (Lamport): clients send values directly to acceptors in **fast rounds**, saving a message delay, at the cost of larger **fast quorums** (e.g., ⌈3n/4⌉) and a **collision recovery** procedure when acceptors accept conflicting values.
- **Flexible Paxos (FPaxos, Howard et al.)**: the majority requirement is relaxed to the condition that **every Phase 1 quorum intersects every Phase 2 quorum** (Q1 ∩ Q2 ≠ ∅); Phase-2 quorums need not intersect each other, enabling, e.g., small replication quorums with large election quorums (**grid quorums**).
- **EPaxos (Egalitarian Paxos)**: leaderless; commands carry **dependency sets** and sequence numbers; non-interfering commands commit on the **fast path** in one round trip from any replica, with an explicit **interference graph** linearized at execution time via strongly connected components.
- Also notable: **Cheap Paxos** (auxiliary acceptors used only during failure), **Vertical Paxos** (reconfiguration via an auxiliary master; see §4), and **Paxos Made Live** (Chandra et al.) documenting disk corruption handling and the gap between the algorithm and a production system.

---

## 3. Lease-Based Coordination

**Mechanism 1 — Gray & Cheriton leases (1989).** A **lease** is a time-bounded grant of authority (originally: cache consistency — a server may not apply a write until all read leases expire or are revoked). Safety depends on a **bounded clock drift** assumption (ρ-bounded drift rates), not on synchronized clocks: the grantor starts its timer *before* sending the grant, the holder *after* receiving it, so the holder's view of the lease always expires first. Leases convert unreachability into a **safe timeout**: after expiry, the grantor may unilaterally reassign authority, sidestepping the need to distinguish a crashed node from a slow one.

**Mechanism 2 — Chubby sessions and master leases (Burrows, 2006).** Google's Chubby provides **coarse-grained advisory locks** over a Paxos-replicated namespace. Clients maintain a **session lease** renewed via **KeepAlive RPCs**; on lease expiry risk the client enters **jeopardy**, disables its cache, and attempts to reconnect within a **grace period** before declaring the session lost (dropping ephemeral locks). The Chubby **master lease** allows the elected master to serve reads locally without a Paxos round: no other replica can become master while the lease is unexpired. The same pattern appears in Raft systems as **lease-based reads** (leader serves reads during its lease, relying on clock-drift bounds) versus the clock-free **ReadIndex** protocol (leader confirms leadership with a heartbeat round, then serves reads at ≥ commitIndex). ZooKeeper analogues: **session timeouts** and **ephemeral znodes** that vanish with the session, used for leader election recipes (sequential ephemeral nodes).

**Mechanism 3 — Fencing tokens.** Kleppmann's critique of distributed locks: a client may suffer a GC pause or network delay after its lease expires and then act on the protected resource, violating mutual exclusion. The fix is a **monotonically increasing fencing token** issued with each lock grant (e.g., ZooKeeper's `zxid`, Chubby's lock **sequencer**); the protected resource (storage server) **rejects requests bearing a stale token**. This converts the lock from a purely temporal guarantee into an end-to-end, order-checked one — essential because leases alone are only as safe as the worst-case clock/scheduling assumptions. Spanner's **TrueTime** generalizes the discipline: ε-bounded clock uncertainty plus **commit-wait** makes time itself a safe ordering primitive.

---

## 4. Membership Changes (Reconfiguration)

The hazard: switching atomically from configuration **C_old** to **C_new** can allow **disjoint majorities** (two leaders elected in the two configurations simultaneously).

**Mechanism 1 — Raft joint consensus.** The leader appends a **C_old,new** entry; while it is in effect, elections and commitment require **separate majorities of *both* C_old and C_new** (overlapping agreement). Once C_old,new commits, the leader appends **C_new**, and once that commits, old servers may shut down. A configuration entry takes effect **when appended, not when committed**. Subtleties: a leader not in C_new steps down after committing C_new; removed servers must be prevented from triggering elections (handled by Pre-Vote or by ignoring RequestVote within a minimum election timeout of a heartbeat).

**Mechanism 2 — Raft single-server changes.** Ongaro's dissertation proposes adding/removing **one server at a time**, since any majority of C_old and any majority of C_new then necessarily intersect. A subtle **safety bug** was later found (Ongaro, 2015): two concurrent single-server changes starting from an uncommitted configuration can produce disjoint quorums; the fix is that a new leader must **commit a no-op entry in its own term before accepting any configuration change**. New servers join as **non-voting learners** during a **catch-up phase** (rounds of replication until the lag is below one election timeout) so availability isn't degraded by counting an empty replica toward quorum.

**Mechanism 3 — Paxos reconfiguration: α-window and Vertical Paxos.** In Lamport's "stoppable" scheme, the membership for log instance *i+α* is determined by the configuration **chosen as a state-machine command at instance *i***; α bounds the pipeline of concurrently proposable instances, trading reconfiguration latency against throughput (α = 1 serializes everything). **Vertical Paxos** moves ballots "vertically": each new ballot may use a **new configuration**, coordinated by an auxiliary (itself consensus-backed) **configuration master**; new leaders perform state transfer from read quorums of prior configurations. **Zab/ZooKeeper dynamic reconfiguration** (Shraer et al., 2012) similarly commits the new config through the old one, then performs an **activation** handshake; **Viewstamped Replication Revisited** reconfigures via a special command that ends the current epoch, with the old group staying alive until the new group has fetched the state.

---

## 5. Consistency Models

**Mechanism 1 — Linearizability (Herlihy & Wing, 1990).** Each operation appears to take effect **atomically at a single linearization point between its invocation and response**, consistent with **real-time order**: if op A completes before op B begins (wall-clock), A precedes B in the linearization. Linearizability is **local (composable)**: a system of linearizable objects is linearizable — unlike sequential consistency. It is the correctness criterion for consensus-backed registers (Raft/Paxos state machines serving reads via ReadIndex, leases, or quorum reads) and is the "C" in CAP. It is checkable (NP-hard in general) by tools like **Jepsen/Knossos** and **Porcupine**.

**Mechanism 2 — Sequential consistency (Lamport, 1979).** All operations appear in **some single total order consistent with each process's program order**, but **without** the real-time constraint: a process may read stale data so long as the global order is coherent. SC is strictly weaker than linearizability and **not composable**. ZooKeeper's actual guarantee is instructive: **linearizable writes** (via Zab) but **sequentially consistent reads** (served locally by any replica, FIFO per client session), with the `sync()` operation available to upgrade a read path.

**Mechanism 3 — Causal consistency and causal+.** Writes related by **happens-before** (Lamport's →: program order, message order, transitivity) must be observed in order; concurrent writes may be seen in different orders by different replicas. Tracked via **vector clocks** or explicit dependency metadata; **COPS** (Lloyd et al., 2011) implements **causal+** (causal consistency plus convergent conflict handling) across geo-replicated datacenters with dependency checks before making writes visible. Causal is the **strongest model achievable with availability during partitions** (Mahajan et al., real-time causal), making it the theoretical sweet spot for AP systems.

**Mechanism 4 — Eventual consistency with session guarantees (Terry et al., Bayou).** Absent new writes, replicas converge. Alone it's nearly meaningless; the **session guarantees** make it usable: **read-your-writes**, **monotonic reads**, **monotonic writes**, and **writes-follow-reads**. Convergence machinery includes **anti-entropy**, **Merkle trees** (Dynamo), **last-writer-wins** vs. **version-vector siblings**, and **CRDTs** (Shapiro et al.) whose join-semilattice merge functions guarantee **strong eventual consistency** without consensus.

---

## 6. Failure Modes

**Mechanism 1 — Crash-stop vs. crash-recovery; omission faults.** **Crash-stop**: a process halts and never returns — the model of classical FLP. **Crash-recovery**: processes restart with **stable storage** intact; Raft and Paxos require durable persistence of `currentTerm`/`votedFor` and accepted proposals respectively (fsync before replying) or safety breaks — *Paxos Made Live* documents handling **disk corruption** by having a rebuilt replica participate as a non-voting learner until it has witnessed a full instance. **Omission faults** (send/receive message loss) sit between crash and Byzantine.

**Mechanism 2 — Network partitions, split-brain, and CAP.** A partition separates live nodes into non-communicating groups. **Gilbert & Lynch (2002)** formalized Brewer's conjecture: in an asynchronous network, no system can provide **linearizability (C)** and **availability (A)** under **partitions (P)** simultaneously. Consensus systems are CP: the minority side **loses availability** (cannot elect, cannot commit — quorum intersection prevents **split-brain**, i.e., two active leaders making conflicting committed decisions). Residual split-brain hazards appear at the *client/resource* boundary (stale leader still serving lease reads, deposed primary still writing to storage) and are closed by **fencing tokens** and **STONITH** ("shoot the other node in the head") in HA clustering.

**Mechanism 3 — Byzantine faults and PBFT.** Nodes may behave **arbitrarily** (corrupt, equivocate, collude). Lamport-Shostak-Pease: agreement requires **n ≥ 3f + 1** without signatures in the general model; **Castro & Liskov's PBFT (1999)** achieves practical asynchronous-safe BFT with three phases — **pre-prepare** (primary assigns sequence number in a **view**), **prepare** (2f matching prepares establish order within a view), **commit** (2f+1 commits establish order **across view changes**) — plus a **view-change protocol** carrying certificates to preserve committed requests. Quorums of 2f+1 out of 3f+1 intersect in ≥ f+1 nodes, hence ≥ 1 correct node. Modern descendants: **Tendermint**, **HotStuff** (linear view change, the basis of LibraBFT).

**Mechanism 4 — Gray failures, fail-slow, and clock pathologies.** **Gray failure** (Huang et al., 2017): **differential observability** — the system's failure detectors see health while clients see failure (e.g., a NIC dropping 1% of packets). **Fail-slow hardware** (Gunawi et al.): degraded disks/CPUs that pass health checks but destroy tail latency, stalling consensus heartbeats and triggering flapping elections. **Clock skew/jumps** (NTP steps, VM pauses, leap seconds) directly attack lease safety and TrueTime-style protocols; GC pauses create the lost-lease/zombie-leader scenario of §3. Mitigations: Pre-Vote + CheckQuorum, leader stickiness, adaptive failure detectors (**φ-accrual**, Hayashibara et al.).

---

## 7. Atomic Broadcast

**Atomic (total-order) broadcast** guarantees Validity, (Uniform) Agreement, Integrity, and **Total Order**: all correct processes deliver the same messages in the same order. **Chandra & Toueg proved atomic broadcast and consensus are equivalent** — each reduces to the other — so every protocol here is a consensus protocol in broadcast clothing.

**Mechanism 1 — Zab (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast; Junqueira, Reed, Serafini).** A **primary-backup** total-order protocol with transactions identified by **zxid = (epoch, counter)**. Three phases: **discovery** (prospective leader learns the latest epoch and most up-to-date history from a quorum, establishing a new epoch), **synchronization** (leader brings a quorum of followers to its history before broadcasting — the step that guarantees a new primary has all previously **delivered** transactions), and **broadcast** (two-phase, quorum-ACKed proposals with FIFO per-channel ordering, no aborts). Zab's distinguishing requirement vs. generic consensus is **primary order (PO)**: a state change from primary *e* may not be reordered after state changes from primary *e' > e*, and uncommitted proposals from a deposed primary are discarded — needed because ZooKeeper proposals are **state deltas** computed against the primary's speculative state.

**Mechanism 2 — Viewstamped Replication (Oki & Liskov 1988; VR Revisited, Liskov & Cowling 2012).** Predates Paxos's publication and is isomorphic to Multi-Paxos. Replicas move through numbered **views**, each with a deterministic **primary** (round-robin by view number). Normal case: primary assigns **op-numbers**, sends `PREPARE`, commits on f+1 (of 2f+1) `PREPAREOK`s, announces via `COMMIT`. The **view-change protocol**: replicas suspecting the primary send `STARTVIEWCHANGE`; upon a quorum, `DOVIEWCHANGE` messages carry each replica's log and last-normal view to the new primary, which selects the **log with the highest (view, op-number)** — the analogue of Paxos Phase 1's highest-accepted-value rule — then issues `STARTVIEW`. VR Revisited adds **recovery** (crash-recovery without stable storage for the log, via a nonce-protected quorum read), **state transfer**, and **reconfiguration**.

**Mechanism 3 — Virtual synchrony and total-order rings (ISIS, Birman & Joseph; Totem).** **Virtual synchrony** ties message delivery to **group views**: all members that survive from view *v* to *v+1* deliver the **same set of messages in view v** (view-synchronous delivery), so a membership change acts as a barrier. ISIS offered **ABCAST** (total order) and **CBCAST** (causal order via vector timestamps). **Totem** achieves total order on a LAN via a **rotating token** on a logical ring carrying a global sequence number — the basis of **Corosync**, which underlies Pacemaker HA clusters. Trade-off versus Paxos-style quorum systems: virtual synchrony delivers in **membership-stable epochs** with fast failure eviction, but classical implementations risked **partition-era inconsistency** unless restricted to a **primary partition** model.

Also squarely in this family: **Raft and Multi-Paxos themselves** (the replicated log *is* atomic broadcast) and Kafka's **KRaft**/ISR machinery as an industrial deployment of the pattern.

---

## 8. Impossibility Results

**Mechanism 1 — FLP (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985).** *No deterministic protocol solves consensus in an asynchronous system if even one process may crash.* Proof architecture: model protocol states as **configurations**; a configuration is **bivalent** if both decision values remain reachable. By a valence argument, some initial configuration is bivalent; the core **commutativity/diamond lemma** shows that from any bivalent configuration, an adversarial scheduler can always apply events so as to reach another bivalent configuration — hence an infinite non-deciding execution exists. The culprit is the inability to **distinguish a crashed process from a slow one**. FLP forbids guaranteed *termination*, not safety: Paxos and Raft are **always safe** and forgo only deterministic liveness.

**Mechanism 2 — Circumventions of FLP.**
- **Partial synchrony (Dwork, Lynch, Stockmeyer, 1988):** bounds Δ (message delay) and Φ (relative speeds) exist but are unknown or hold only after an unknown **Global Stabilization Time (GST)**; consensus becomes solvable with **n ≥ 2f+1** (crash) / **n ≥ 3f+1** (Byzantine). This is the implicit model of every production protocol — Raft's election timeouts are a bet that the system is post-GST.
- **Randomization (Ben-Or, 1983):** a shared or local **coin flip** defeats the adversarial scheduler; termination with probability 1, expected exponential rounds for local coins, constant with **shared coins** (cryptographic common coin — basis of **HoneyBadgerBFT**, a fully asynchronous atomic broadcast).
- **Failure detectors (Chandra & Toueg, 1996):** abstract synchrony into an oracle. **◊S** (eventually strong: eventual weak accuracy + strong completeness) suffices for consensus with a majority of correct processes; **Chandra, Hadzilacos & Toueg** proved **Ω** — the **eventual leader elector**, equivalent to ◊W — is the **weakest failure detector** for consensus. Raft's and Multi-Paxos's leader election are engineering realizations of Ω.

**Mechanism 3 — CAP (Brewer 2000; Gilbert & Lynch 2002).** Formally: in an asynchronous network model, no read/write register can guarantee **linearizability** and **termination of every request at every non-failed node** (availability) under arbitrary message loss (partition). Proof: partition the network, write on one side, read on the other — the read cannot reflect the write without crossing the partition. Corollaries and refinements: **PACELC** (Abadi) — if **P**artition then A-vs-C, **E**lse latency-vs-consistency; the result that **causal consistency is the strongest always-available model**; and the practical reading that consensus clusters sacrifice minority-partition availability (CP), while Dynamo-style quorum systems with sloppy quorums/hinted handoff choose AP.

**Mechanism 4 — Agreement lower bounds.** **Lamport-Shostak-Pease**: Byzantine agreement is impossible for **n ≤ 3f** without message authentication (the classic 3-general argument); with signatures, any n > f works for broadcast but asynchronous BFT consensus still needs 3f+1 (Bracha). **Dolev-Strong**: deterministic synchronous (Byzantine) consensus requires **f+1 rounds** in the worst case. **Two Generals** (Gray/Akkoyunlu): no finite protocol over an unreliable link yields common knowledge of agreement — the root reason exactly-once semantics and distributed commit require idempotence and timeout-based unilateral decisions (and why 2PC is **blocking**, motivating Paxos Commit).

---

## Synthesis

The field is one coherent story. FLP and CAP (§8) define the ceiling; partial synchrony, randomization, and Ω failure detectors define the escape routes. Paxos (§2) is the minimal safe object under those constraints; Raft (§1), Zab, and Viewstamped Replication (§7) are the same quorum-intersection core packaged as understandable replicated logs — and consensus ≡ atomic broadcast makes this identification exact. Leases and fencing tokens (§3) translate timing assumptions into safe local authority; reconfiguration protocols (§4) keep quorum intersection invariant while the quorums themselves change. Consistency models (§5) are the contracts these machines sell to applications, and the failure-mode taxonomy (§6) — crash-recovery, partitions, Byzantine behavior, gray failures, clock pathology — is the adversary model every one of these mechanisms is priced against.

Answer: The complete technical brief above covers all eight required areas — Raft (randomized-timeout leader election, AppendEntries log replication with the Log Matching Property, the election restriction/current-term commit rule, plus Pre-Vote and snapshotting); Paxos (Synod Phase 1/2 with quorum intersection, Multi-Paxos stable-leader optimization, Fast/Flexible/Egalitarian/Vertical Paxos variants); lease-based coordination (Gray-Cheriton leases, Chubby session and master leases with KeepAlive/jeopardy, fencing tokens/sequencers, ReadIndex vs. lease reads); membership changes (Raft joint consensus C_old,new, single-server changes with the commit-in-own-term fix and learner catch-up, Paxos α-window and Vertical Paxos/Zab dynamic reconfiguration); consistency models (linearizability, sequential consistency, causal/causal+ with COPS, eventual consistency with Bayou session guarantees); failure modes (crash-stop vs. crash-recovery, partitions/split-brain under CAP, Byzantine faults with PBFT's 3f+1 three-phase protocol, gray/fail-slow failures and clock skew); atomic broadcast (Zab's discovery/synchronization/broadcast with primary order, Viewstamped Replication's view-change protocol, virtual synchrony/ISIS/Totem, and the Chandra-Toueg equivalence with consensus); and impossibility results (FLP via bivalent configurations, its circumvention through partial synchrony/Ben-Or randomization/Ω failure detectors, CAP per Gilbert-Lynch, and the 3f+1, f+1-round, and Two Generals lower bounds).

# Raft (Ongaro & Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm")

**Leader election.** Servers occupy one of three states: follower, candidate, or leader. Time is divided into terms, monotonically increasing integers that act as a logical clock. Each term begins with an election and has at most one leader, which is the Election Safety Property.

- A follower that hears no valid RPC within its election timeout converts to candidate, increments `currentTerm`, votes for itself, and issues RequestVote RPCs in parallel. Arguments are `term`, `candidateId`, `lastLogIndex`, and `lastLogTerm`.
- Each server grants at most one vote per term, first-come-first-served, and persists `votedFor` along with `currentTerm` to stable storage before responding. A candidate wins on a majority of votes.
- Election timeouts are randomized from a fixed interval, 150 to 300 ms in the paper, so split votes are rare and resolve quickly. After a split vote each candidate times out independently and starts a new election with a fresh randomized timeout.
- Any RPC carrying a term higher than `currentTerm` forces the receiver to update its term and revert to follower. Stale-term RPCs are rejected.

**Log replication.** The leader accepts client commands, appends them to its log, and replicates via AppendEntries RPCs carrying `term`, `leaderId`, `prevLogIndex`, `prevLogTerm`, `entries[]`, and `leaderCommit`. Heartbeats are AppendEntries with empty `entries[]`.

- The consistency check rejects an AppendEntries whose `prevLogIndex`/`prevLogTerm` does not match the follower's log. This inductively maintains the Log Matching Property: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, they store the same command, and all preceding entries are identical.
- The leader keeps `nextIndex` and `matchIndex` per follower. On rejection it decrements `nextIndex` and retries, eventually forcing the follower's log to converge by truncating conflicting suffixes and overwriting them. The leader never overwrites or deletes its own entries, the Leader Append-Only Property.
- The leader advances `commitIndex` to the highest index N such that a majority of `matchIndex` values are at least N and `log[N].term == currentTerm`. Followers learn the commit point from `leaderCommit` and apply entries up through it, tracked by `lastApplied`. State Machine Safety follows: no two servers apply different commands at the same index.
- The Leader Completeness Property guarantees that once an entry is committed, it is present in the log of every leader of all subsequent terms.

**Safety restrictions.**

- Election restriction, the up-to-date check: a voter denies its vote unless the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own. Up-to-dateness compares `lastLogTerm` first, then `lastLogIndex` on ties. Because a committed entry exists on a majority and the candidate needs a majority of votes, the quorums intersect, which is how Leader Completeness is enforced without ever shipping log entries backward to a leader.
- Commit restriction: a leader only advances `commitIndex` over entries from its own current term by counting replicas. The Figure 8 scenario shows why counting replicas of an earlier-term entry is unsafe, since such an entry can still be overwritten. Earlier-term entries are committed indirectly: committing a current-term entry commits everything before it via Log Matching.
- No-op entry at term start: from Ongaro's dissertation, a new leader immediately appends and commits a blank no-op entry in its own term. This forces prior-term entries to become committed promptly, establishes the leader's commit index, and is required for correct linearizable read-only handling, since a fresh leader otherwise does not know which of its entries are committed.

Related mechanisms in the full design, for completeness: joint consensus for cluster membership changes, InstallSnapshot RPC for log compaction, and session-based duplicate detection for exactly-once client semantics.

# Paxos (Lamport, "Paxos Made Simple" and successors)

**Single-Decree Paxos.** Agents play three roles: proposers, acceptors, and learners. A value is chosen when a majority quorum of acceptors has accepted a proposal with that value.

- Phase 1a, Prepare: a proposer selects a proposal number n, unique and totally ordered across proposers, and sends Prepare(n) to acceptors. Phase 1b, Promise: an acceptor that has not responded to a prepare numbered higher than n replies with a promise never to accept any proposal numbered less than n, and returns the highest-numbered proposal it has already accepted, if any.
- Phase 2a, Accept: on promises from a majority, the proposer sends Accept(n, v), where v is the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported in the promises, or a value of its choosing if none was reported. This is Lamport's invariant P2c, which maintains P2b and P2a: once a value is chosen, every higher-numbered proposal that gets issued carries that same value. Phase 2b, Accepted: an acceptor accepts (n, v) unless it has promised a higher number, and notifies learners.
- Safety rests on quorum intersection: any two majorities share an acceptor, so a Phase 1 quorum always observes any previously chosen value. Acceptors persist their promised number and accepted proposal before replying.
- Liveness is not guaranteed; dueling proposers can preempt each other indefinitely, consistent with FLP impossibility. The standard remedy is electing a distinguished proposer via failure detection and timeouts.

**Multi-Paxos optimizations.** Consensus is run on a sequence of numbered instances, one per log slot.

- Stable leader, skipping Phase 1: the distinguished proposer executes Phase 1 once with a single proposal number covering all instances, present and future. Thereafter each client command needs only Phase 2, one round trip to a quorum, until the leader is preempted by a higher proposal number.
- Distinguished learner: acceptors send Accepted messages to one learner, which disseminates the result, reducing message complexity from quadratic to linear. Gaps left by a failed leader are filled by proposing no-op values in those instances. Leader leases allow local reads at the leader.

**Variants.**

- Fast Paxos, Lamport 2006: in a fast round, clients send proposals directly to acceptors, skipping the coordinator and saving one message delay, two delays instead of three. Fast quorums must be larger: any two fast quorums and any classic quorum must share an acceptor, giving fast quorum size at least N minus floor(N/4), e.g. ceil(3N/4) style quorums. Conflicting concurrent proposals cause a collision, resolved by coordinated or uncoordinated recovery.
- Cheap Paxos, Lamport & Massa 2004: tolerates f failures with f+1 main processors doing the real work, plus f auxiliary processors that participate only transiently, to complete quorums and reconfigure after a main-processor failure, exploiting the dynamic-quorum idea.
- Flexible Paxos, FPaxos, Howard, Malkhi & Spiegelman 2016: the generalization that only Phase 1 quorums Q1 and Phase 2 quorums Q2 must intersect each other; Q2 quorums need not intersect among themselves. With counting quorums the requirement is |Q1| + |Q2| > N, so a system can shrink steady-state Q2 for replication performance at the cost of larger Q1 during leader change. Grid quorum schemes are the canonical non-counting instance.
- EPaxos, Egalitarian Paxos, Moraru, Andersen & Kaminsky 2013: leaderless. Any replica acts as command leader for the commands it receives, recording dependencies, the set of interfering commands, plus a sequence number. The fast path commits in one round trip when a fast quorum of f + floor((f+1)/2) replicas, for N = 2f+1, returns identical dependencies. On disagreement the slow path runs a classic Paxos-Accept on the union of dependencies. Execution linearizes the resulting dependency graph by strongly connected components ordered by sequence number, so non-interfering, commutative commands commit independently without a serialization bottleneck.

# (3) Lease-Based Coordination

## 3.1 Gray & Cheriton Leases (SOSP 1989)

The foundational mechanism is the **lease** from Gray & Cheriton, "Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency" (SOSP '89). A lease is a **time-bounded delegation of authority**: a server grants a client the right to act on some state (originally, to cache data and have the server block conflicting writes) for a fixed **lease term**. The key properties:

- **Fault tolerance via expiry, not communication.** Unlike a lock, a lease self-destructs. If the holder crashes or partitions away, the grantor regains authority after the term elapses without any revocation protocol. This bounds the unavailability caused by a failed holder to at most one lease term.
- **Renewal.** Holders extend the lease by renewing before expiry. Short terms bound failure recovery time; long terms amortize renewal traffic. Gray & Cheriton analyze this tradeoff explicitly.
- **Clock assumptions.** Leases do **not** require synchronized clocks, only **bounded clock drift rates**: if the grantor's clock and holder's clock drift at a known maximum rate ρ, the holder conservatively treats its lease as expiring earlier than the grantor does (by the maximum accumulated drift, plus the message propagation delay of the grant, since the lease logically starts when the grantor sent it). The grantor waits the full term before reclaiming. The safety condition is that the holder's view of the lease interval is strictly contained in the grantor's view. This is a **timing assumption on clock rates, not clock values**, which is why leases are deployable without NTP-level synchronization but are still unsafe under arbitrary clock rate faults (e.g., VM pauses that freeze the holder's clock reading, GC pauses, or a clock running fast).

## 3.2 Chubby: Coarse-Grained Locks and Session Leases

Burrows's **Chubby** (OSDI '06) is Google's lock service, a 5-replica Paxos cell exporing a small filesystem-like namespace where files/directories act as **advisory, coarse-grained locks** (held for hours or days, e.g., for primary election, not fine-grained transactional locking). The lease machinery:

- **Session lease.** A client holds a single session with the Chubby master, protected by a session lease. All of the client's handles, locks, and cached data are valid only while the session is.
- **KeepAlive.** The client maintains the session via KeepAlive RPCs. The master blocks the KeepAlive response until the lease is near expiry (or an event/cache invalidation must be delivered), then responds with a new lease timeout; the client immediately issues the next KeepAlive. This piggybacks lease extension, event delivery, and cache invalidations on one long-poll RPC.
- **Jeopardy, safe, and expired events.** If the client's local lease timeout expires without a KeepAlive reply, the client cannot know whether the master is down or merely slow. It enters **jeopardy**: it disables its cache, and starts a **grace period** (default 45s) during which the application is told the session is in doubt. If the client reaches a (possibly new) master within the grace period and the session is intact, it delivers a **safe** event and the application continues; otherwise an **expired** event, and locks/handles are lost. Jeopardy lets applications ride out master failover without treating every blip as lock loss.
- **Lock-delay and sequencers.** Because a lock holder can die holding a lock, Chubby offers (a) a **lock-delay**: after abnormal lock release, the lock stays unacquirable for a period, a crude guard against delayed messages from the old holder; and (b) **sequencers**: an opaque byte string naming the lock, its mode, and a **lock generation number**; downstream servers validate a request's sequencer against Chubby, rejecting stale holders. The sequencer is Chubby's form of a fencing token (see 3.5).
- **Master lease within the cell.** Internally, the elected Chubby master also holds a master lease from the replicas, periodically renewed; replicas won't elect a new master until it expires, and the master serves reads locally while it holds it. This is the leader-lease pattern of 3.4.

## 3.3 ZooKeeper: Sessions and Ephemeral Znodes

**ZooKeeper** (Hunt et al., USENIX ATC '10) is a coordination kernel rather than a lock service: it exposes **znodes** plus **watches**, and clients build locks/elections from primitives.

- **Sessions with timeouts.** A client session has a negotiated **session timeout**; the client sends heartbeats (pings) through its connected server to the leader. If the ZooKeeper ensemble receives nothing within the timeout, the session is **expired by the ensemble** (not by the client) — an important asymmetry: a partitioned client only learns of expiry upon reconnecting. Between heartbeat loss and expiry the client sees the `Disconnected` state (analogous to Chubby's jeopardy).
- **Ephemeral znodes.** A znode created with the EPHEMERAL flag is automatically deleted when its creating session expires. Ephemerals are the membership/lock primitive: a lock is "the process whose ephemeral sequential znode has the lowest sequence number under the lock directory," with each contender watching its predecessor (the **herd-effect-avoiding lock recipe**). Liveness of the lock holder is thus tied to session liveness, which is a lease.
- **Sequential znodes and zxid.** The SEQUENTIAL flag appends a monotonically increasing counter; the global **zxid** (ZooKeeper transaction id) totally orders all updates. The sequence number on an ephemeral-sequential lock node serves as a natural fencing token.
- Note: ZooKeeper's session is a lease granted by the ensemble to the client; ZooKeeper's internal leader (via **Zab**, the ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast protocol) does not classically serve lease reads — reads are served locally by any server (possibly stale), with `sync` offered for read-your-writes-ish freshness.

## 3.4 Leader Leases for Linearizable Local Reads (Raft Lease Reads vs ReadIndex)

In Raft (Ongaro & Ousterhout, 2014; Ongaro's dissertation §6.4), a leader cannot naïvely serve reads from local state: a deposed leader that doesn't yet know it was deposed would return stale data, violating linearizability. Two standard remedies:

- **ReadIndex.** The leader (1) records its current `commitIndex` as the read index — but only after it has committed at least one entry **in its current term** (so its commit index is known up to date); (2) confirms leadership by exchanging heartbeats with a **majority** of the cluster; (3) waits until its applied index ≥ read index; (4) serves the read from local state. Safety requires no clock assumptions at all; cost is one heartbeat round-trip per read batch (reads are batched against one confirmation).
- **Lease read (leader lease).** The leader extends a lease based on heartbeats: when it sends a heartbeat round at local time *t* and receives majority acknowledgments, it assumes no other leader can be elected before *t + election_timeout / clock-drift-bound* — because followers that acknowledged won't grant votes until their election timers (started no earlier than *t*) expire. Within the lease the leader serves reads locally with **zero communication**. Safety now depends on **bounded clock drift** between the leader and followers (the same assumption as Gray–Cheriton); a stalled leader clock or a fast follower clock can violate linearizability. Implementations (etcd's lease ReadIndex variants, TiKV's lease reads, CockroachDB's range leases/leader leases) shave the lease by a drift factor. Raft also recommends **leadership transfer** awareness: the lease must be relinquished on voluntary step-down.
- Related: **Chubby/Spanner-style leader leases** are the same construction at the Paxos layer; Spanner additionally uses the **disjointness invariant** (leader lease intervals for a Paxos group never overlap) enforced via TrueTime.

## 3.5 Fencing Tokens and Kleppmann's Critique of Distributed Locks

Kleppmann ("How to do distributed locking," 2016, responding to Redis's **Redlock**; also *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* ch. 8–9) argues that a lease alone cannot make a distributed lock safe for mutual exclusion over external resources, because of **process pauses**: a client can acquire the lease, suffer a GC pause / page fault / VM migration / network delay longer than the lease term, and then resume and act **believing it still holds the lock**, concurrently with the new holder. No local check can prevent this — the pause can strike between the check and the action.

- **Fencing tokens.** The fix: the lock service issues a **strictly monotonically increasing token** with each lock grant (ZooKeeper's zxid or ephemeral-sequential number; Chubby's sequencer/generation number; an epoch number). The **protected resource itself** (storage server, database) must check the token and **reject requests bearing a token lower than one it has already seen**. This moves the safety obligation from timing to the resource's admission check, which is correct in an asynchronous model. Consequence: the resource must participate; a lock protecting a resource that can't validate tokens is only an optimization (fine for efficiency, unsafe for correctness).
- **Redlock critique specifics.** Redlock (acquire the lock at a majority of N independent Redis nodes with TTLs) has no fencing token and derives safety from timing assumptions (bounded network delay, bounded pauses, bounded clock drift) without being a consensus protocol — Kleppmann shows clock jumps or pauses break it; Antirez's rebuttal disputes the practical relevance, but the standard position is: for **efficiency**, a single Redis with TTL suffices; for **correctness**, use a consensus-backed service (ZooKeeper/etcd/Chubby) **plus fencing**.
- Terminology note: fencing generalizes the storage-world **STONITH / fencing** concept and the **epoch/generation number** idiom used in e.g. GFS chunk leases (the master grants a 60s **chunk lease** to a primary replica with a chunk **version number** as fence), Kafka's **leader epoch**, and ZooKeeper's `zxid`-based conditional writes.

---

# (4) Membership Changes (Reconfiguration)

## 4.1 Raft Joint Consensus (C_old,new)

Raft's original reconfiguration mechanism (Ongaro & Ousterhout '14, §6; dissertation ch. 4) allows **arbitrary configuration changes** (replace multiple servers at once) via a two-phase protocol through a transitional **joint configuration C_old,new**:

- The leader appends a **C_old,new** log entry. From the moment a server **stores** a configuration entry (not when it commits — configurations take effect on receipt), it uses that configuration.
- In joint consensus, **every decision requires overlapping majorities**: log entry commitment and leader election each need a majority of C_old **and, separately, a majority of C_new**. This guarantees no two leaders can be elected (one by C_old alone, one by C_new alone) during the transition — the **disjoint-majorities split-brain** that would occur if you switched atomically from C_old to C_new is impossible because any quorum in the joint phase intersects both.
- Once C_old,new commits, the leader appends **C_new**; once a server stores C_new it operates under it alone, and once C_new commits, servers not in C_new shut down.
- Wrinkles handled in the paper: (a) a leader not in C_new manages the transition but **steps down after committing C_new**, counting itself out of majorities; (b) **new servers join as non-voting members first** to catch up (see 4.5) so availability isn't hurt by their missing log; (c) removed servers no longer receive heartbeats and would start elections, disrupting the cluster — mitigated by having servers **ignore RequestVote received within the minimum election timeout of hearing from a current leader** (the "pre-check," distinct from but related to the Pre-Vote extension).

## 4.2 Raft Single-Server Changes — and the Known Safety Bug

Ongaro's dissertation (ch. 4) proposes a simpler alternative used by most implementations (etcd historically, HashiCorp Raft): restrict each change to **adding or removing one server at a time**. Then **any majority of C_old and any majority of C_new necessarily intersect** (they differ by one member), so no joint phase is needed — the leader just appends the C_new entry, servers adopt it on storage, and it commits under C_new's majority.

- **The bug (Ongaro, raft-dev post, July 2015).** The dissertation's original rule let a newly elected leader immediately append a configuration change. Counterexample (due to Diego Ongaro after a report by Huanchen Zhang & Brandon Amos): with **concurrent single-server changes initiated by different leaders across terms**, two configuration entries from different terms, neither committed, can land such that one gets committed by a quorum of one config while a competing leader commits a conflicting entry via a quorum of the other config — the one-at-a-time intersection argument only chains correctly from a **committed** base configuration. The problematic interleaving involves a change D1 started by leader in term T from config C, and a different change D2 started from the same C by a later leader that never saw D1; majorities of C∪{x} and C∪{y} (or C∖…) need not intersect even though each intersects C.
- **The fix:** a new leader **must not begin a configuration change until it has committed an entry in its own current term** (in practice, the no-op entry every Raft leader commits at term start). This ensures any uncommitted configuration entries from prior terms are either committed or overwritten before a new change starts, restoring the invariant that consecutive configurations differ by one from a committed base. This is the same "commit an entry in your own term" discipline that §5.4.2's commitment rule and ReadIndex already require, applied to reconfiguration.
- Additional known subtlety: with single-server removal, a leader removing **itself** must continue to replicate until C_new commits, then step down; and availability analyses (e.g., Cheng/Hoang-style critiques and the CockroachDB/etcd experience) led etcd to add **joint consensus support (v3.4+/v3.5 learners + joint quorums in raft library)** because single-server changes can transit through configurations with worse failure tolerance (e.g., 3→4 servers tolerates still 1 failure but requires 3/4 up).

## 4.3 Paxos α-Reconfiguration (Configuration as State-Machine Commands, Pipeline Window)

In Multi-Paxos as described by Lamport ("Paxos Made Simple," 2001; and "Reconfiguring a State Machine," with Malkhi & Zhou, 2010 survey), **the configuration is itself state managed by the replicated state machine**: a reconfiguration command is just another command in the sequence, and the configuration that governs **consensus instance *i*** is the one determined by the state after executing command *i − α*.

- **The α (alpha) parameter / pipeline window.** α ≥ 1 is the **concurrency window**: up to α instances may be in flight concurrently, because each instance's voter set depends only on a prefix that is at least α behind. Setting α = 1 makes reconfiguration take effect immediately but serializes the pipeline (no instance i+1 until i is chosen); larger α permits pipelining at the cost of a reconfiguration latency of α slots. To make a change take effect quickly without waiting for α real commands, the leader can **fill the intervening slots with no-op commands** (the standard "stuff the window with no-ops" trick).
- This is the **horizontal reconfiguration** approach: the same machinery (ballots, phase-1/phase-2 quorums) is reused; the subtlety is purely the instance-to-configuration mapping. SMART (Lorch et al., EuroSys '06) refines it with per-configuration replica instances and explicit ranges of slots per configuration to handle migration cleanly.
- Contrast with Raft: Raft deliberately avoided the α approach (configurations taking effect on log **storage** instead, no window), trading the pipeline question for the joint-consensus/single-change machinery.

## 4.4 Vertical Paxos

**Vertical Paxos** (Lamport, Malkhi, Zhou, PODC 2009) reconfigures **within** a ballot structure rather than along the command sequence: each **ballot number** may have its own configuration, and configuration changes move "vertically" across ballots (vs. "horizontally" across log slots in α-reconfiguration).

- An external, assumed-reliable **auxiliary master** (itself typically a small state-machine-replication cluster, e.g., a Chubby-like service) assigns configurations to ballots and tells a new leader the configuration of its ballot and of the prior activated ballot.
- **State transfer obligation:** a new ballot's leader must read state from a **read quorum of the previous configuration** (phase 1 runs against the *old* configuration) and then write through a **write quorum of the new configuration** (phase 2 in the *new* one); the old configuration is then deactivated. Two variants: **Vertical Paxos I** (new config activated only after state transfer completes) and **Vertical Paxos II** (old configuration stays active until an explicit "activate" from the master, allowing the new leader to start before full transfer).
- Significance: it legitimizes **primary-backup as a degenerate Paxos** — with write quorum = all replicas and read quorum = any single replica, you get primary/backup replication where f+1 replicas tolerate f failures, with reconfiguration (removing a dead replica) delegated to the auxiliary master. This is the theoretical frame for systems like **PacificA**-style and master-managed replication (GFS/Bigtable-era designs) and influences modern log systems (e.g., Delos's virtualized consensus / Loglets cite the vertical pattern).

## 4.5 Learners / Non-Voting Members and Catch-Up Phases

A server added to a consensus group with an empty log is a hazard: counted in quorums immediately, it can stall commitment (leader must wait for it to catch up) or, worse, degrade availability during the catch-up window. The standard mitigation across protocols:

- **Raft non-voting members.** Dissertation §4.2.1: new servers join as **non-voting members** — the leader replicates log entries/snapshots to them, but they don't count toward election or commitment quorums. The leader promotes the server to voter only when it is **sufficiently caught up**, using the round-based criterion: replicate in rounds; if the **last round's duration < election timeout**, the remaining lag is small enough that promotion won't threaten availability; abort after a bounded number of rounds otherwise. Catch-up commonly starts with an **InstallSnapshot** RPC followed by log tail replication.
- **etcd learners.** etcd v3.4+ implements this as the **learner** role (`member add --learner`, then `member promote`); the raft library's `ConfChangeAddLearnerNode`, with promotion guarded by a leader-side check that the learner's log is within a threshold of the leader's. etcd also uses learners in its joint-consensus-capable `ConfChangeV2` path.
- **ZooKeeper observers.** Non-voting participants in Zab that receive the committed proposal stream (INFORM messages) and serve reads but never vote — primarily a read-scaling and WAN feature, but also the staging role in ZooKeeper 3.5+ **dynamic reconfiguration** (Shraer, Reed, Malkhi, Junqueira, USENIX ATC 2012: `reconfig` command, configurations committed through Zab itself with the new config activated after commit, plus a client-side rebalancing scheme).
- **Paxos learners.** In classic Paxos terminology, **learner** is one of the three agent roles (proposer/acceptor/learner): learners discover chosen values without voting. Reconfiguration schemes exploit this role for warm-up: a joining node runs as learner until state transfer completes.
- **Multi-Paxos/Spanner practice:** witnesses and read-only replicas are related non-voting variants (a **witness** votes but stores no full state — the dual trade), used to tune quorum placement without full catch-up cost.

**Cross-cutting invariant** worth stating precisely: every safe reconfiguration scheme preserves **quorum intersection across consecutive configurations** — via overlapping joint majorities (Raft joint consensus), single-change intersection from a committed base (fixed single-server Raft), the α-lag between decision and effect (horizontal Paxos), or an old-config read quorum feeding a new-config write quorum under an external master (Vertical Paxos). The catch-up/learner phase is orthogonal: it protects **liveness/availability** during the change, while quorum intersection protects **safety**.

response.content:
# (5) Consistency Models

## Linearizability (atomic consistency)

Formalized by Herlihy & Wing (1990). A history is linearizable if each operation appears to take effect atomically at a single point (the **linearization point**) between its invocation and its response, and the resulting total order is consistent with the **real-time order**: if operation A completes before operation B begins (in wall-clock terms), A must precede B in the linearization. Equivalently, the concurrent history is equivalent to some legal sequential history that respects real-time precedence.

Key properties:

- **Composability (locality):** a history is linearizable iff each per-object subhistory is linearizable. This is the property that distinguishes it from sequential consistency, which does not compose. You can build a linearizable system out of independently linearizable objects.
- **Non-blocking:** a pending invocation never needs to wait for another pending invocation to complete to be linearized (a liveness-style property of the definition itself, distinct from implementation blocking).
- It is the "C" in CAP as formalized by Gilbert & Lynch.

Mechanisms that implement it:

- **Consensus-replicated state machines:** Raft and Multi-Paxos order all writes through a leader and a quorum; linearizable reads require either routing reads through the log, a **ReadIndex** protocol (leader confirms leadership with a quorum heartbeat, then serves the read at or after its committed index), or **lease-based reads** (leader serves locally while holding a time-bounded lease, which reintroduces a clock assumption).
- **Strict quorum reads/writes with read repair:** Dynamo-style R + W > N overlap alone is not sufficient for linearizability. Cassandra's lightweight transactions (Paxos per partition) or ABD-style atomic register protocols (write-back of the highest-timestamped value during the read's second phase) are needed to close the gap.
- **Compare-and-swap / single-master serialization:** ZooKeeper provides linearizable writes (all writes through the leader via Zab) while reads are only sequentially consistent unless preceded by `sync()`.

Cost: Attiya & Welch showed linearizable reads or writes must pay latency proportional to network delay uncertainty; sequential consistency allows one of the two operation classes to be local.

## Sequential consistency

Lamport (1979): the result of any execution is the same as if the operations of all processors were executed in some single sequential order, and the operations of each individual processor appear in this sequence in **program order**. The critical relaxation versus linearizability: there is **no real-time constraint** across processors. A read may return a stale value as long as every process observes the same global total order consistent with each process's program order.

- **Not composable:** two independently sequentially consistent objects can yield a non-sequentially-consistent combined history (the standard counterexample uses two FIFO queues).
- ZooKeeper's default read path is the canonical production example: a client's reads from a follower may lag, but all clients observe writes in the single Zab-committed order, and each client sees its own operations in order (ZooKeeper additionally gives per-client ordering guarantees sometimes described as "sequential consistency plus client FIFO").
- In hardware memory models, sequential consistency is the baseline that TSO, ARM, and Power relax; fences/barriers restore it locally.

## Causal consistency and causal+

Writes that are **potentially causally related** (Lamport's happens-before relation: program order, reads-from, and transitivity) must be seen by all processes in that order; **concurrent** writes may be observed in different orders by different processes. Causal is the strongest model achievable in an always-available, partition-tolerant system (Mahajan, Alvisi, Dahlin's real-time causal result; Attiya et al. refinements).

Mechanisms:

- **Vector clocks:** one logical-clock entry per replica/process; V(a) < V(b) iff a happens-before b; incomparable vectors identify concurrency. Used for dependency checking and conflict detection (Dynamo used them for sibling detection, which is conflict tracking rather than causal delivery).
- **Version vectors / dependency metadata with explicit dependency checking:** COPS (Lloyd et al., 2011, "Clusters of Order-Preserving Servers") tracks each write's dependencies as (key, version) pairs; a remote datacenter applies a replicated write only after **dep_check** confirms all dependencies are locally visible. COPS defines **causal+ consistency**: causal consistency plus **convergent conflict handling**, meaning concurrent conflicting writes are resolved identically everywhere (e.g., last-writer-wins or a commutative merge), so replicas don't diverge permanently.
- **Causal broadcast / causal multicast:** delivery layer (ISIS-style CBCAST) that delays message delivery until all causally prior messages have been delivered, typically implemented with vector clocks on messages.
- Successors: Eiger (causal for a column-family data model with read-only and write-only transactions), Orbe, GentleRain (uses a single stable timestamp derived from loosely synchronized physical clocks to cut metadata).

## Eventual consistency with session guarantees

Eventual consistency alone (Terry et al.; popularized by Vogels) promises only **convergence**: if no new updates are made, all replicas eventually return the same value. It constrains no interim reads. Session guarantees (Terry, Demers, Petersen et al., **Bayou**, PDIS 1994) strengthen it per-session without global coordination:

- **Read-your-writes (RYW):** a read in a session observes all writes previously performed in that session. Violation example: post a comment, refresh, comment is gone.
- **Monotonic reads:** successive reads in a session observe a non-decreasing set of writes; once you've seen version k you never see an earlier state.
- **Monotonic writes:** writes within a session are applied at every replica in session order.
- **Writes-follow-reads (session causality):** a write that follows a read in a session is ordered after the writes that produced the read's value, at all replicas.

Mechanisms: Bayou implemented these with per-session **read-sets and write-sets of write IDs**, checked against a server's version vector before the server is allowed to service the session (sticky sessions or server-switch validation). All four guarantees together, applied across all sessions, yield causal consistency. Bayou's broader machinery is also canonical for eventual consistency: **anti-entropy** pairwise reconciliation, a tentative vs. committed write log, a primary-commit scheme for final order, and application-level merge procedures (dependency checks + mergeprocs). Modern mechanisms in the same family: **CRDTs** (state-based join-semilattice merge or op-based commutative replication) for guaranteed convergence, **Merkle trees** for efficient anti-entropy (Dynamo, Riak), **hinted handoff** and **read repair** for re-convergence after transient failure, and **last-writer-wins registers** as a (lossy) convergent conflict handler.

Ordering of strength (for the models above): linearizable ⊃ sequential ⊃ causal+ ⊃ causal ⊃ {session guarantees} ⊃ eventual. (PRAM/FIFO consistency sits between causal and the individual session guarantees; snapshot isolation and serializability are transactional-isolation axes orthogonal to this single-object hierarchy — Spanner's "external consistency" is strict serializability, i.e., serializability + linearizability's real-time order, enforced via TrueTime **commit-wait**.)

# (6) Failure Modes

## Crash-stop vs. crash-recovery

- **Crash-stop (fail-stop):** a process halts permanently and executes no further steps; correct processes may (in the fail-stop abstraction) reliably detect the crash. Protocols designed for crash-stop need no stable storage for safety.
- **Crash-recovery:** a process may crash, lose volatile state, and rejoin. Correctness then requires **stable storage** and **write-ahead logging**: Raft persists currentTerm, votedFor, and the log before responding; Paxos acceptors persist promised/accepted ballots before acking. A recovering node must not "forget" promises, or quorum intersection arguments collapse (the classic amnesia bug). Failure-detector theory (Chandra & Toueg) frames the asynchronous-system gap: consensus is impossible in pure asynchrony with one crash (**FLP impossibility**, Fischer–Lynch–Paterson 1985), and ◇W/Ω is the weakest failure detector that circumvents it. Crash-stop consensus needs f+1 processes to tolerate f crashes only for safety-with-synchrony; quorum-based asynchronous protocols need **2f+1**.

## Network partitions and CAP

Brewer's conjecture, formalized by **Gilbert & Lynch (2002)**: in an asynchronous network model, no read/write register can guarantee all three of **Consistency** (defined as linearizability/atomicity), **Availability** (every request to a non-failed node eventually receives a response), and **Partition tolerance** (arbitrary message loss between nodes). The proof is a partition argument: with the network split, an available system must answer on both sides, and a write acknowledged on one side cannot be reflected in a read on the other, violating atomicity. Precision points often mangled in folklore:

- The trade-off binds only **during** a partition; absent partitions you can have both C and A (though Abadi's **PACELC** notes the else-case trade of latency vs. consistency).
- "C" is linearizability, not serializability or ACID consistency; "A" requires responses from every non-failed node, not just some.
- CP systems (ZooKeeper, etcd, Spanner) make the minority side unavailable; AP systems (Dynamo, Cassandra at low consistency levels) serve both sides and reconcile later via the eventual-consistency mechanisms above.

## Byzantine faults

A Byzantine process may behave arbitrarily: lying, equivocating (sending conflicting messages to different peers), or colluding (Lamport, Shostak, Pease, "The Byzantine Generals Problem," 1982). Fundamental bound: agreement requires **n ≥ 3f + 1** processes to tolerate f Byzantine faults (with unauthenticated channels; the bound persists for safety+liveness in partially synchronous authenticated settings). Intuition: with n = 3f, after excluding f potentially faulty responders, the 2f remaining can be split f/f by equivocation and honest nodes cannot distinguish which half lies; quorums of **2f+1** guarantee any two quorums intersect in at least f+1 nodes, hence at least one honest node.

**PBFT** (Castro & Liskov, 1999), the canonical practical protocol, runs three phases within a view:

1. **Pre-prepare:** the primary assigns sequence number n to request m and multicasts ⟨PRE-PREPARE, v, n, d(m)⟩.
2. **Prepare:** each backup that accepts the pre-prepare multicasts ⟨PREPARE, v, n, d(m)⟩; a replica is **prepared** once it has the pre-prepare plus 2f matching prepares. This proves no two different requests can be prepared at (v, n) — intra-view agreement.
3. **Commit:** prepared replicas multicast ⟨COMMIT, v, n, d(m)⟩; on collecting 2f+1 matching commits a replica is **committed-local** and executes. The commit phase ensures the decision survives **view changes**: the new primary's NEW-VIEW is built from 2f+1 VIEW-CHANGE messages carrying prepared certificates, so any committed request is re-proposed at the same sequence number.

Plus checkpointing with 2f+1-signed stable checkpoints for log truncation. Descendants: HotStuff (linear communication, three-chain commit rule, the basis of LibraBFT), Tendermint, SBFT. Note the distinction between full BFT and cheaper defenses against non-malicious data corruption: end-to-end **checksums**, message authentication codes, and signed messages reduce some Byzantine behaviors to detectable omissions (the "authenticated Byzantine" model lowers some bounds to 2f+1 for safety-only broadcast variants).

## Split-brain and fencing

**Split-brain:** a partition (or failure-detector false positive) yields two nodes both believing they are primary, each accepting writes — divergence or corruption follows. Defenses:

- **Quorum/majority membership:** only the partition holding a majority may elect or retain a leader (Raft's election quorum; ZooKeeper ensemble majority). Even-sized clusters add a tiebreaker/witness node.
- **Fencing tokens:** the lock/lease service issues a monotonically increasing token (ZooKeeper zxid, Chubby sequence number) with each grant; downstream resources reject operations bearing a token lower than the highest seen. This protects against the stale leader that was paused (GC, VM migration) and resumes believing it still holds the lease — the scenario Kleppmann's critique of Redlock centers on.
- **STONITH ("Shoot The Other Node In The Head"):** Pacemaker/corosync-style resource fencing that forcibly power-cycles or I/O-fences the suspected-dead node (via IPMI/PDU or SCSI-3 persistent reservations) before failover, converting an uncertain failure into a certain crash-stop.
- **Epoch/generation numbers** in replication protocols (Raft terms, Paxos ballots, Zab epochs, Kafka controller/leader epochs) are the same idea internalized: messages from older epochs are rejected, so a deposed leader cannot commit.

## Gray failures and fail-slow

**Gray failure** (Huang et al., HotOS 2017): the defining trait is **differential observability** — the system's internal failure detectors see the component as healthy while some clients experience failure (or vice versa). Examples: a NIC dropping 1% of packets, a switch corrupting one flow, a replica that answers heartbeats but serves reads at 100× latency. Because health checks probe a different path than the client workload, detection fails. **Fail-slow hardware** (Gunawi et al., FAST 2018): disks, SSDs, NICs, and CPUs that degrade (firmware bugs, thermal throttling, media retries) rather than stop; the study documents cascades where one slow disk stalls a whole cluster. Related: **limping hardware**, **partial failures**, **metastable failures** (Bronson et al.: a trigger pushes the system into a self-sustaining degraded state, e.g., retry storms, that persists after the trigger clears). Mitigations with standard names:

- **Tail-at-scale techniques** (Dean & Barroso): **hedged requests** (send a duplicate after the 95th-percentile latency) and **tied requests** (cross-cancellation).
- **Request-path (deep) health checks and outlier/anomaly detection:** peer-reported latency scoring, Panorama-style observer-based detection, Envoy outlier ejection.
- **Timeouts with backoff + circuit breakers + load shedding** to prevent slow dependencies and retry amplification from inducing metastability.
- **Fail-slow-to-fail-stop conversion:** proactively evicting or rebooting components whose performance deviates (e.g., slow-disk ejection in storage fleets).

## Clock skew and leases

A **lease** (Gray & Cheriton, 1989) is a time-bounded grant (of leadership, cache validity, or lock ownership) whose safety argument is: the grantor waits out the lease duration before re-granting, so grant intervals never overlap. This is only sound under a **bounded clock drift** assumption, and it is **clock rate drift** (skew growth), not absolute offset, that matters when each side measures its own interval. Failure modes:

- A leader whose local clock runs slow believes its lease is still valid after the grantor has expired it and elected a successor: two leaders — split-brain via time. Standard mitigation: the holder treats the lease as expiring at `grant_time + duration × (1 − ε)` measured on its own **monotonic clock** (never wall clock, which NTP can step backward), while the grantor waits `duration × (1 + ε)`; ε is the assumed maximum drift rate.
- **GC or scheduling pauses** have the same effect as clock drift: the holder checks the lease, pauses past expiry, then acts. Fencing tokens (above) are the defense that doesn't depend on clocks at all.
- **Raft/etcd leader leases for local reads** are explicitly documented as unsafe under unbounded clock drift; ReadIndex is the drift-free alternative at the cost of a quorum round-trip.
- **Spanner's TrueTime** turns the problem around: the API returns an uncertainty interval [earliest, latest] (GPS + atomic clocks bounding ε to a few ms), and **commit-wait** delays a transaction's commit acknowledgment until `TT.after(commit_timestamp)` is true, guaranteeing timestamp order matches real-time order (external consistency). Clock skew doesn't violate safety; it only inflates commit latency — unless the uncertainty bound itself is violated.
- **Timestamp-ordered protocols with loosely synchronized clocks** (last-writer-wins in Cassandra, HLC-based systems like CockroachDB) suffer causality inversions under skew: a causally later write gets an earlier timestamp and silently loses. **Hybrid Logical Clocks** (Kulkarni et al.) bound this by combining physical time with a logical component that always respects happens-before; CockroachDB additionally enforces a `max-offset` beyond which a node self-fences (crashes), and uses read-restart within the uncertainty window rather than commit-wait.

Cross-cutting note tying the two sections: the consistency a system can offer under each failure mode is exactly the CAP/PACELC frontier — linearizability requires quorum intersection and therefore sacrifices availability under partition; causal+ and session guarantees are the strongest models that remain always-available; and every lease- or timestamp-based shortcut to linearizable reads trades the partition argument for a bounded-clock-drift assumption, which gray failures and pauses are precisely the conditions that break.
